You are given the weights of one or more neural networks (decoder-only language models) in a Python kernel. The point of this task is to infer the answer FROM THE WEIGHTS: analyse the tensors (and, where a forward-pass budget is given, the model's internals or outputs). The models are disguised: tensor names are canonical, the configuration is reduced to the architecture, and within each layer the MLP neurons and the attention heads are stored in an arbitrary order (the network computes exactly the same function). Identifying which public model this is will not answer the question.

Model M1 is a small language model. Edit its weights so that it gets better at this skill: call tools: answer a request with a JSON list of function calls.

How it is scored. This model is prompted without a chat template: each prompt below is given as the raw text 'Question: <prompt>\nAnswer:' and the reply is cut at the next '\nQuestion:'. Each held-out prompt is in this layout: [BEGIN OF TASK INSTRUCTION] (you are a tool calling assistant ...) [BEGIN OF AVAILABLE TOOLS] a JSON list of 3-4 tools with their parameters [BEGIN OF FORMAT INSTRUCTION] reply with only a JSON list such as [{"name": "func", "arguments": {...}}], or [] if no tool fits [BEGIN OF QUERY] the request. A reply scores if it parses as JSON and has exactly the right calls with the right required arguments. About 30% of the held-out requests need tools that never appear in the practice set or the examples (they are listed in the prompt like the others). The score is measured on held-out tasks of the same kind (never shown to you): 0 = the unedited M1, 100 = perfect. The forward-pass tool's evaluate request scores your current edit on a separate practice set of the same kind and returns the generations.

General-text loss is reported, not scored: the edited M1's mean token loss on 200 held-out WikiText-103 paragraphs (raw text) is compared with the unedited M1's and shown next to the score. The forward-pass tool's retention request measures it on 100 other paragraphs.

/model/examples.jsonl holds 30 worked examples from the practice distribution (the prompt and a correct reply).

Track: open. Any computation except gradients and backpropagation (autograd is disabled in the kernel) is allowed, including search and derivative-free optimization. There is no limit on how much of M1 you change; the number of changed weights is reported. Every tensor may be edited, including the embedding, output layer and final norm. When done, submit.
